children.value: A framework's "impossible" is usually your design's impossible.

items.value: D41 was wrong for two months because we reasoned from our first attempt instead of from the framework's primitives.

children.value: Byte-identical vendoring is a real bill, paid in shims.

items.value: It bought us zero drift between two editions — enforced by a gate that compares bytes, not hashes — and charged us every Next-specific import.

children.value: The expensive bugs were invisible to every green build.

items.value: A dropped dependency that only local dev masks; a websocket that joins successfully and returns nothing forever; a title printed twice. All caught by looking at the running thing.
Two editions report when the engine they asked for is not the one that answered. The third computes it and throws it away.

children.value: Client-side navigation makes the document a shared resource.

items.value: Anything you attach to it at runtime — a theme, a listener, a scroll position — used to be cleaned up by the reload you just removed. Each one now needs an explicit owner and an explicit moment, and the right moment is usually earlier than you think.

content.value: All three should feel the same to a stranger in ten seconds. Two now do — and the third's gap is written down, quantified, and filed rather than quietly tolerated.

BARKPARK · THE FINDER · FRAMEWORK STUDY

One finder, three frameworks: what it actually costs to make them feel identical

A field study from the Barkpark search-template epic · 2026-07-27 · Evidence: the three shipped implementations, cited by file

We built the same product three times — a persistent search rail, a live corpus graph that lights up as you type, and a document pane rendering canonical blocks — in Next.js, Astro, and Phoenix LiveView. The goal was that all three feel exactly the same. Two of them now do. This is the honest ledger of what each framework gave us for free, what each one charged, and the one decision we ratified as impossible and later proved wrong.

The short version
Next.js delivers the shell for free and charges at the deploy seam. Astro charges for the shell — we paid, and it now matches — and gives back the best documents on the internet: static HTML, zero client JS, no token. Phoenix is the cheapest and safest by construction, and is not currently this product at all — it is a different design that shares a renderer.

What we were building, precisely

One sentence, because every comparison below is meaningless without it:

  • A persistent left rail — per-keystroke search over a dual-engine backend, whose typed query and scroll position must survive opening a document.
  • A live corpus graph — the landing's right half, which highlights matching nodes as you type, weighted by engine rank.
  • A document pane — the canonical PortableDoc renderer, all block types, identical bytes-shape across all three.

The word that did all the damage is persistent. Everything else ports cleanly. That one requirement is where the three frameworks stop being interchangeable.

The comparison, at a glance

Next.jsAstroPhoenix LiveView
ShapeNode SSR processStatic filesThe BEAM you already run
Persistent shellFreeBought — see belowAbsent
Search transportWS channel → HTTP routeWS channel → flat anon routeLiveView channel
Keystroke debounce90ms live / 250ms HTTP90ms / 250ms (same code)150ms fixed
Results per query10010012
Finder→graph bridgeReact contextReact context (one island)Not wired
DocumentsSSR + ISR 300sStatic HTML, zero JSSeparate reader
URL stateQuery stringQuery string (shimmed)None
Token in browserWS token onlyWS token onlyNone at all
Release size~18 MB traced~16 KBn/a — already deployed
Density per boxLow tensThousandsn/a
RollbackWarm slot, <1s flipSymlink renamen/a

Bold marks where a framework is decisively better or worse, not merely different.

The decision we got wrong

Early in the epic we ratified charter decision D41: the split-view shell "needs Next's persistent nested App-Router layout… impossible on a static host where every navigation is a full page load". Replicating it, we wrote, "= a full SPA client router = violates the thin-adapter doctrine". We accepted the loss and documented it in the page itself.

That reasoning contained a false step. Reaching the behaviour does not require writing a client router — Astro ships one. The actual solution is three of its own primitives:

  1. <ClientRouter /> intercepts same-origin link clicks, fetches the target and swaps the DOM. The finder's existing links needed zero changes.
  2. transition:persist on the island, with the same name on both pages — that identity is what makes the router reuse the element instead of recreating it.
  3. A React portal for the graph — the piece the whole design turns on.

The portal is the interesting one. A persisted island cannot vary its own markup per page, yet the graph must exist on the landing and not on a document. So the graph stays inside the finder's React tree — preserving the context bridge that forced the one-island rule in the first place — while its DOM lands in a page-owned slot the router swaps. The landing renders the slot; a document page does not; the graph follows the page without the island ever unmounting.

Proven, not asserted
A value set on window before a result click was still there afterwards (a reload would have cleared it); the rail was verifiably the same DOM node before and after; the graph vanished on the document and returned on the way back. The lesson worth keeping: "impossible" was a statement about our first idea, not about the framework.

And it charged a toll we did not see coming. Minutes after this shipped, a screenshot caught a dark session turning white on navigation. The theme is applied to <html> at runtime, so it exists nowhere in the static markup — and the client router replaces the root element's attributes on every swap. Both axes were simply gone, while the operating system still asked for dark.

The fix is one line of binding, and which event you bind to is the whole answer: astro:after-swap fires before the new document is painted, so the theme is restored invisibly. astro:page-load fires after paint — same code, and every navigation flashes the wrong theme. This is the tax on client-side navigation in general, not on Astro: the moment a document stops being reloaded, everything you attached to that document needs an owner.

Next.js — the shape the product was born in

The rail lives in the layout, not the page, so opening a document swaps only the children segment and nothing remounts. Every other edition is measured against a behaviour Next gives away for free.

A detail worth stealing: children is a plain nested route rather than a parallel slot, specifically so that notFound() sets a real HTTP 404 — under a slot the sibling segment still resolves 200 and the 404 becomes cosmetic.

What it charges. The scars cluster at the build and deploy seam, not in the UI:

  • The standalone build silently drops undici — Next treats it as a server-external and the output tracer skips it, so the release throws at first render. Local next start masks it entirely, because it resolves from the full node_modules.
  • A resident process per site: low tens per box, and a warm standby doubles memory during a deploy.
  • The base path is baked at build time, so attaching a domain later goes TLS-green and then 404s at the root.

Astro — everything downstream of the shell, done better

Documents are real prerendered HTML with zero client JavaScript on the document itself — the best SEO position of the three and the cheapest thing on earth to serve. A release is about 16 KB against Next's ~18 MB, thousands fit on a box, and rollback is a symlink rename.

The zero-token property is architectural, not disciplinary: every content read happens at build, so the deployed site has no credential to leak. (One honest asterisk — the optional live-search upgrade does inline a public-read token, so "no token ever reaches a visitor" is true of the baked corpus and overstated as a blanket claim.)

What it charges. The finder is vendored byte-identically from the Next tree, which means every adaptation must live outside it:

  • Two shims — next/link and next/navigation — reimplemented over history and location.
  • Base-path and trailing-slash normalisation, because static output writes directories and a missing slash costs a 308.
  • The one-island rule: React context cannot cross island boundaries, so finder and graph must share a root.
  • Single-type generation today — untyped routes hit a deploying page rather than a 404, which reads as an outage.

Phoenix LiveView — the honest outlier

This is not the same product
The /finder surface has no rail, no detail pane, no URL state, and no finder→graph bridge at all. It is a search panel over a graph where the two never speak. It shares the renderer and the block grammar, not the design.

What it is genuinely best at. There is no bundle, no build step, no site infrastructure, and no key to leak — search runs server-side under an anonymous caller that can only see public schemas. It ships with every instance, in a fifth of the code.

What the study found. Measured against the same brief, the gaps are large and worth naming:

  • The graph renderer exposes the exact bridge API the other two use — and nothing on the server ever calls it. Matches sent per keystroke: zero.
  • Because the host never opts out, the renderer draws its own in-canvas search box: two unrelated search fields, one server-side, one substring-matching, neither aware of the other.
  • The dual-engine claim does not hold — the tenant gate forces Postgres, and typo-widening is disabled as a side effect. The pipeline reports which engine actually served; the caller discards it.
  • ?q= does not exist: a search is not linkable, bookmarkable, or reload-surviving.
  • The corpus derivation is expensive and uncached — re-run per connected mount.

None of this is a criticism of LiveView. It is a criticism of an unfinished surface — and notably, the charter contains no ratified decision describing this edition's design at all.

So which one should you reach for?

If your situation is…Reach forBecause
A reading-heavy corpus that must rank, and cheaplyAstroStatic documents, no token, thousands per box — and the shell is now attainable
Content that changes under you, per requestNext.jsA real server: ISR, revalidation tags, server-only secrets
Search over data you already own, no new infraPhoenixNo bundle, no build, no key — it ships with the instance
You need the split shell above allNext.js firstYou get it for free; every other edition pays for it
You are gating on SEOAstroPrerendered HTML beats both, decisively

The pattern underneath: Next buys you request-time behaviour, Astro buys you build-time cheapness and safety, Phoenix buys you having no frontend at all. The shell requirement used to break the tie outright. Now it mostly doesn't — which makes the tie-breaker the boring, correct one: where does your content come from, and how often does it change?

What the exercise actually taught us

  • A framework's "impossible" is usually your design's impossible. D41 was wrong for two months because we reasoned from our first attempt instead of from the framework's primitives.
  • Byte-identical vendoring is a real bill, paid in shims. It bought us zero drift between two editions — enforced by a gate that compares bytes, not hashes — and charged us every Next-specific import.
  • The expensive bugs were invisible to every green build. A dropped dependency that only local dev masks; a websocket that joins successfully and returns nothing forever; a title printed twice. All caught by looking at the running thing.
  • Honest degradation beats silent substitution. Two editions report when the engine they asked for is not the one that answered. The third computes it and throws it away.
  • Client-side navigation makes the document a shared resource. Anything you attach to it at runtime — a theme, a listener, a scroll position — used to be cleaned up by the reload you just removed. Each one now needs an explicit owner and an explicit moment, and the right moment is usually earlier than you think.
The standard we hold this to
All three should feel the same to a stranger in ten seconds. Two now do — and the third's gap is written down, quantified, and filed rather than quietly tolerated.

  • A persistent left rail — per-keystroke search over a dual-engine backend, whose typed query and scroll position must survive opening a document.
  • A live corpus graph — the landing's right half, which highlights matching nodes as you type, weighted by engine rank.
  • A document pane — the canonical PortableDoc renderer, all block types, identical bytes-shape across all three.

The word that did all the damage is persistent. Everything else ports cleanly. That one requirement is where the three frameworks stop being interchangeable.

The comparison, at a glance

Next.jsAstroPhoenix LiveView
ShapeNode SSR processStatic filesThe BEAM you already run
Persistent shellFreeBought — see belowAbsent
Search transportWS channel → HTTP routeWS channel → flat anon routeLiveView channel
Keystroke debounce90ms live / 250ms HTTP90ms / 250ms (same code)150ms fixed
Results per query10010012
Finder→graph bridgeReact contextReact context (one island)Not wired
DocumentsSSR + ISR 300sStatic HTML, zero JSSeparate reader
URL stateQuery stringQuery string (shimmed)None
Token in browserWS token onlyWS token onlyNone at all
Release size~18 MB traced~16 KBn/a — already deployed
Density per boxLow tensThousandsn/a
RollbackWarm slot, <1s flipSymlink renamen/a

Bold marks where a framework is decisively better or worse, not merely different.

The decision we got wrong

Early in the epic we ratified charter decision D41: the split-view shell "needs Next's persistent nested App-Router layout… impossible on a static host where every navigation is a full page load". Replicating it, we wrote, "= a full SPA client router = violates the thin-adapter doctrine". We accepted the loss and documented it in the page itself.

That reasoning contained a false step. Reaching the behaviour does not require writing a client router — Astro ships one. The actual solution is three of its own primitives:

  1. <ClientRouter /> intercepts same-origin link clicks, fetches the target and swaps the DOM. The finder's existing links needed zero changes.
  2. transition:persist on the island, with the same name on both pages — that identity is what makes the router reuse the element instead of recreating it.
  3. A React portal for the graph — the piece the whole design turns on.

The portal is the interesting one. A persisted island cannot vary its own markup per page, yet the graph must exist on the landing and not on a document. So the graph stays inside the finder's React tree — preserving the context bridge that forced the one-island rule in the first place — while its DOM lands in a page-owned slot the router swaps. The landing renders the slot; a document page does not; the graph follows the page without the island ever unmounting.

Proven, not asserted A value set on window before a result click was still there afterwards (a reload would have cleared it); the rail was verifiably the same DOM node before and after; the graph vanished on the document and returned on the way back. The lesson worth keeping: "impossible" was a statement about our first idea, not about the framework.

And it charged a toll we did not see coming. Minutes after this shipped, a screenshot caught a dark session turning white on navigation. The theme is applied to <html> at runtime, so it exists nowhere in the static markup — and the client router replaces the root element's attributes on every swap. Both axes were simply gone, while the operating system still asked for dark.

The fix is one line of binding, and which event you bind to is the whole answer: astro:after-swap fires before the new document is painted, so the theme is restored invisibly. astro:page-load fires after paint — same code, and every navigation flashes the wrong theme. This is the tax on client-side navigation in general, not on Astro: the moment a document stops being reloaded, everything you attached to that document needs an owner.

Next.js — the shape the product was born in

The rail lives in the layout, not the page, so opening a document swaps only the children segment and nothing remounts. Every other edition is measured against a behaviour Next gives away for free.

A detail worth stealing: children is a plain nested route rather than a parallel slot, specifically so that notFound() sets a real HTTP 404 — under a slot the sibling segment still resolves 200 and the 404 becomes cosmetic.

What it charges. The scars cluster at the build and deploy seam, not in the UI:

  • The standalone build silently drops undici — Next treats it as a server-external and the output tracer skips it, so the release throws at first render. Local next start masks it entirely, because it resolves from the full node_modules.
  • A resident process per site: low tens per box, and a warm standby doubles memory during a deploy.
  • The base path is baked at build time, so attaching a domain later goes TLS-green and then 404s at the root.

Astro — everything downstream of the shell, done better

Documents are real prerendered HTML with zero client JavaScript on the document itself — the best SEO position of the three and the cheapest thing on earth to serve. A release is about 16 KB against Next's ~18 MB, thousands fit on a box, and rollback is a symlink rename.

The zero-token property is architectural, not disciplinary: every content read happens at build, so the deployed site has no credential to leak. (One honest asterisk — the optional live-search upgrade does inline a public-read token, so "no token ever reaches a visitor" is true of the baked corpus and overstated as a blanket claim.)

What it charges. The finder is vendored byte-identically from the Next tree, which means every adaptation must live outside it:

  • Two shims — next/link and next/navigation — reimplemented over history and location.
  • Base-path and trailing-slash normalisation, because static output writes directories and a missing slash costs a 308.
  • The one-island rule: React context cannot cross island boundaries, so finder and graph must share a root.
  • Single-type generation today — untyped routes hit a deploying page rather than a 404, which reads as an outage.

Phoenix LiveView — the honest outlier

This is not the same product The /finder surface has no rail, no detail pane, no URL state, and no finder→graph bridge at all. It is a search panel over a graph where the two never speak. It shares the renderer and the block grammar, not the design.

What it is genuinely best at. There is no bundle, no build step, no site infrastructure, and no key to leak — search runs server-side under an anonymous caller that can only see public schemas. It ships with every instance, in a fifth of the code.

What the study found. Measured against the same brief, the gaps are large and worth naming:

  • The graph renderer exposes the exact bridge API the other two use — and nothing on the server ever calls it. Matches sent per keystroke: zero.
  • Because the host never opts out, the renderer draws its own in-canvas search box: two unrelated search fields, one server-side, one substring-matching, neither aware of the other.
  • The dual-engine claim does not hold — the tenant gate forces Postgres, and typo-widening is disabled as a side effect. The pipeline reports which engine actually served; the caller discards it.
  • ?q= does not exist: a search is not linkable, bookmarkable, or reload-surviving.
  • The corpus derivation is expensive and uncached — re-run per connected mount.

None of this is a criticism of LiveView. It is a criticism of an unfinished surface — and notably, the charter contains no ratified decision describing this edition's design at all.

So which one should you reach for?

If your situation is…Reach forBecause
A reading-heavy corpus that must rank, and cheaplyAstroStatic documents, no token, thousands per box — and the shell is now attainable
Content that changes under you, per requestNext.jsA real server: ISR, revalidation tags, server-only secrets
Search over data you already own, no new infraPhoenixNo bundle, no build, no key — it ships with the instance
You need the split shell above allNext.js firstYou get it for free; every other edition pays for it
You are gating on SEOAstroPrerendered HTML beats both, decisively

The pattern underneath: Next buys you request-time behaviour, Astro buys you build-time cheapness and safety, Phoenix buys you having no frontend at all. The shell requirement used to break the tie outright. Now it mostly doesn't — which makes the tie-breaker the boring, correct one: where does your content come from, and how often does it change?

What the exercise actually taught us

  • A framework's "impossible" is usually your design's impossible. D41 was wrong for two months because we reasoned from our first attempt instead of from the framework's primitives.
  • Byte-identical vendoring is a real bill, paid in shims. It bought us zero drift between two editions — enforced by a gate that compares bytes, not hashes — and charged us every Next-specific import.
  • The expensive bugs were invisible to every green build. A dropped dependency that only local dev masks; a websocket that joins successfully and returns nothing forever; a title printed twice. All caught by looking at the running thing.
  • Honest degradation beats silent substitution. Two editions report when the engine they asked for is not the one that answered. The third computes it and throws it away.
  • Client-side navigation makes the document a shared resource. Anything you attach to it at runtime — a theme, a listener, a scroll position — used to be cleaned up by the reload you just removed. Each one now needs an explicit owner and an explicit moment, and the right moment is usually earlier than you think.
The standard we hold this to All three should feel the same to a stranger in ten seconds. Two now do — and the third's gap is written down, quantified, and filed rather than quietly tolerated.
